Ohio U Bobcats.previous_hc_experience: None as a head coach beyond an interim spell. The Coaching Carousel records that 'new' head coach is a loose term here, as John Hauser was the assistant head coach and defensive coordinator before Brian Smith was placed on leave at the end of the regular season, and the team pages record him as interim head coach for the Frisco Bowl win over UNLV.
Ohio U Bobcats.dc: Kurt Mattix, returning after a season in Charlotte with Tim Albin.
Ohio U Bobcats.oc_status: Returning — the Stability Score table (p. 43) awards 3 points for a returning offensive coordinator.
Ohio U Bobcats.dc_status: New — the Stability Score table (p. 43) awards 0 points for a returning defensive coordinator, the role Hauser vacated on his promotion, with Kurt Mattix returning to it.
Ohio U Bobcats.play_caller: Not addressed in guide by name.
Ohio U Bobcats.offensive_scheme: Not addressed in guide as a named scheme.
Ohio U Bobcats.defensive_scheme: Not addressed as a named scheme. The guide puts last season's 22 sacks in context — 36, 36 and 35 over the previous three seasons, making 22 the fewest since the ill-fated 2021 season and its 17.
Ohio U Bobcats.run_pass: Not addressed as a stated split.
Ohio U Bobcats.qb_development: Treated as a programme phenomenon rather than an individual coach's record. The guide describes a generational run at the position since Tyler Tettleton arrived in 2009, offering several possible causes — scouting and talent evaluation, the system, programme stability, or outright good luck — and notes Ohio's three all-time leading passers all come from the last 20 years in Tettleton, Nathan Rourke and Kurtis Rourke. Its verdict on the successors is that the bar is set so high virtually any of them is likely to fall short.
Ohio U Bobcats.continuity: Offensive coordinator returns; head coach, defensive coordinator and quarterback all change. The Stability Score table (p. 43) prints 0, 3, 0 and 0, plus 0 for 5 returning starters, totalling 3.
Ohio U Bobcats.staff_turnover: A further link in a chain of internal promotions. The guide traces Tim Albin to Brian Smith to Hauser and wonders whether one of these transitions eventually has a big impact, noting Kurt Mattix returns as coordinator after a season in Charlotte with Albin. It also finds it interesting that Hauser was co-defensive coordinator at Miami of Ohio, making him one of the few external hires in recent seasons — while admitting it is unsure whether that matters.
Ohio U Bobcats.prior_school: Miami of Ohio for Hauser's earlier coordinator work, and Charlotte for Mattix's intervening season. The Coaching Carousel adds that Hauser has spent his entire FBS career in the MAC and is a Columbus native and Wittenberg University graduate. On the roster the guide records Matt Vezza from New Hampshire.
Ohio U Bobcats.portal_recruiting: Rated poorly. The guide records a noticeably lacklustre portal class, while the Coaching Carousel expects Hauser to keep getting good in-house talent from a top-10, borderline top-five, state for high school football.
Ohio U Bobcats.vsin_assessment: Continuity as the theme, and a warning that it may finally run out. The Coaching Carousel says there's something to be said about continuity in college football in 2026, notes Hauser follows Smith and Albin, who were both on the staffs of their predecessors, and expects his Ohio roots to keep local talent coming. The team pages read the handover from Frank Solich to Albin causing a one-year blip as unsurprising, then suspect this could be the year a transition has a big impact — listing one returning starter on offense, the loss of multi-year quarterback Parker Navarro, the loss of near-1,400-yard rusher Sieh Bangura, and a lacklustre portal class. Its specific scenario is a transitional year while developing three-star Columbus-area freshman Levi Davis.
Ohio U Bobcats.strengths: Offensive-coordinator continuity, a head coach who has been in the programme and already won a bowl in charge, a returning defensive coordinator who knows the system from earlier, deep Ohio recruiting roots, and a documented programme-level record of producing quarterbacks.
Ohio U Bobcats.concerns: One returning starter on offense with an all-new offensive line, the loss of the quarterback, a near-1,400-yard rusher and the top four receivers including a 1,000-yard pass-catcher, a lacklustre portal class, the top two tacklers and top defensive back gone, and a sack total already at its lowest since 2021.
Ohio U Bobcats.betting: Not addressed in guide as an explicit market recommendation tied to coaching.
Ohio U Bobcats.carousel_summary: Adam Burke starts by qualifying the label: 'new' head coach is a loose term here, as Hauser was the assistant head coach and DC for the Bobcats before HC Brian Smith was placed on leave at the end of the regular season. He then makes the broader point — there's something to be said about continuity in college football in 2026, and Hauser follows Smith and Tim Albin, who were both on the staffs of their predecessors. He grounds the hire regionally: Hauser has spent his entire FBS career in the MAC and is plenty familiar with the Buckeye State as a Columbus native and Wittenberg University grad, so he should be able to keep getting good in-house talent from a top-10, borderline top-five, state for high school football.

Sacramento State Hornets.previous_hc_experience: Almost none. The Coaching Carousel records that Alonzo Carter hasn't been a head coach since 2016 at Contra Costa Junior College, and that he was on Brent Brennan's staffs at both San Jose State and Arizona, serving most recently as assistant head coach and running backs coach.
Sacramento State Hornets.oc_status: New — the Stability Score table (p. 44) awards 0 points for a returning offensive coordinator.
Sacramento State Hornets.dc_status: New — the Stability Score table (p. 44) awards 0 points for a returning defensive coordinator.
Sacramento State Hornets.play_caller: Not addressed in guide by name.
Sacramento State Hornets.offensive_scheme: Changing, and the guide flags the discontinuity explicitly: Brennan Marion's up-tempo offense produced 33.8 points per game, but the scheme will be different this season, with the very few returning offensive players facing a more traditional offense.
Sacramento State Hornets.defensive_scheme: Named. The guide records returning defenders having to learn a 3-3-5 stack.
Sacramento State Hornets.tempo: Expected to fall — the outgoing scheme was up-tempo and the incoming one is described as more traditional.
Sacramento State Hornets.run_pass: Not addressed as a stated split.
Sacramento State Hornets.qb_development: Not addressed as a record. The guide records Carson Conklin returning to the place where he started in 2024 after transferring to Fresno State when Marion took over.
Sacramento State Hornets.continuity: None. The Stability Score table (p. 44) prints 0 for the head coach, 0 for the offensive coordinator, 0 for the defensive coordinator, 0 for the quarterback and 0 for 6 returning starters — a total of 0.
Sacramento State Hornets.staff_turnover: Complete, alongside the programme's move to FBS and to the MAC.
Sacramento State Hornets.prior_school: San Jose State and Arizona under Brent Brennan for Carter, and Contra Costa College for his only previous head-coaching job. Florida for Eric Kiesau and Northern Arizona for Adam Clark.
Sacramento State Hornets.portal_recruiting: Rated well. 247Sports graded Sacramento State's portal class second in the MAC, and the guide describes a roster of JUCO transfers and discarded players.
Sacramento State Hornets.vsin_assessment: An odd hire by the Carousel's reckoning, and an unknown by the team pages' own admission. The Coaching Carousel calls Carter a Brent Brennan disciple in some respects, notes he was already coaching high school ball when Brennan was playing for UCLA, and — given the wild commitment to the basketball programme with head coach Mike Bibby and GM Shaquille O'Neal — says Carter, a one-time backup dancer for MC Hammer, seems like an odd hire by comparison, while adding that the Oakland native is said to be a great mentor and resource for students. The team pages present him as holding a strong reputation for mentoring players and assisting them off the field as much as on it, state their honest limits — they do not know how the team will fare in close games or what his clock management will look like — and assume the team will play extremely hard every week.
Sacramento State Hornets.strengths: A portal class graded second in the MAC, a returning quarterback coming back to where he started, a head coach with a strong mentoring reputation, and a schedule the guide says softens the travel shock — no back-to-back road games outside the end of the season, and only one departure from California before October 10.
Sacramento State Hornets.concerns: A Stability Score of 0 with six returning starters, entirely new playbooks on both sides with returning defenders learning a 3-3-5 stack, a head coach who has not led a programme since 2016 at junior-college level, the loss of a 1,200-yard rusher and a 755-yard receiver, major questions in the trenches on both sides, and a simultaneous jump to FBS and into the MAC's travel.
Sacramento State Hornets.betting: Not addressed in guide as an explicit market recommendation tied to coaching. Its answer to whether the Hornets will be competitive is 'maybe', with the caveat that it probably will not show in the standings.
Sacramento State Hornets.carousel_summary: Adam Burke establishes two facts before anything else: yes, Sacramento State is an FBS team now, and yes, they are in the MAC. He then places the coach — Carter is a Brent Brennan disciple in some respects, though he was already coaching high school ball when Brennan was playing for UCLA, and he was on Brennan's staffs at both San Jose State and Arizona, most recently as assistant head coach and running backs coach. He notes the gap in the résumé: he hasn't been a head coach since 2016 at Contra Costa Junior College. His comparison is institutional — given the wild commitment to the basketball team with head coach Mike Bibby and GM Shaquille O'Neal, Carter, a one-time backup dancer for MC Hammer, seems like an odd hire by comparison. He closes on the counterweight: the Oakland native is said to be a great mentor and resource for students.

Toledo Rockets.previous_hc_experience: Extensive, and unusual in its route. The Coaching Carousel records that Mike Jacobs, a Maumee native from northwestern Ohio, worked his way up the hard way — head coach at Division II Notre Dame College and Lenoir-Rhyne before an FCS opportunity at Mercer — and calls it kind of rare to see a head coach with this sort of path, as many have been coordinators or position coaches at the FBS level, usually from a Power Four school at some point. It records him at 94-23 as a head coach with back-to-back FCS Playoff appearances at Mercer.
Toledo Rockets.oc: Cris Reisert, the former Tiffin and Ohio Dominican head coach.
Toledo Rockets.dc: Jahmal Brown, a Cleveland native who came from Youngstown State.
Toledo Rockets.oc_status: New — the Stability Score table (p. 44) awards 0 points for a returning offensive coordinator.
Toledo Rockets.dc_status: New — the Stability Score table (p. 44) awards 0 points for a returning defensive coordinator.
Toledo Rockets.play_caller: Not addressed in guide by name.
Toledo Rockets.offensive_scheme: Projected from the coordinator's and head coach's previous numbers rather than named: Mercer produced 6.8 yards per play last season with a balanced approach that ranked third nationally in yards per game, 4.9 yards per carry on more than 400 rushing attempts, and over 3,800 passing yards. The guide expects a lean on the run at the outset.
Toledo Rockets.defensive_scheme: Not named, but its character is projected in detail. The guide expects aggression under Jahmal Brown and reasons from Mercer: that group allowed only 3.4 yards per carry but 5.7 yards per play because it got burned for explosives in the passing game, had 42 sacks in 12 games yet generated only 15 takeaways, and its 96 tackles for loss show how heavily it pursued the run and rushed the passer — while leaving an evasive quarterback the chance to burn them.
Toledo Rockets.run_pass: Balanced by design, with an initial lean on the run. The guide also corrects for game state in reading Toledo's own past tendencies — the Rockets may have been a little more run-heavy, but that reflects protecting a lot of leads, some of them big, and this year's team will not have last year's defense, so the game state itself is unknown.
Toledo Rockets.continuity: None. The Stability Score table (p. 44) prints 0 for the head coach, 0 for the offensive coordinator, 0 for the defensive coordinator, 0 for the quarterback and 0 for 6 returning starters — a total of 0.
Toledo Rockets.staff_turnover: Complete, and the guide marks the scale of the break: for the first time since 2016 Toledo will not play for Jason Candle, and for the first time since 2009 Candle is not with the programme at all, having taken the UConn job. It emphasises the regional coherence of the replacement staff — Jacobs a northwest Ohio native, Reisert the former Tiffin and Ohio Dominican head coach, and Brown a Cleveland native from Youngstown State.
Toledo Rockets.prior_school: Mercer, comprehensively — Jacobs plus transfers including running back CJ Miller and receiver Adjatay Dabbs, and Mercer defenders who already know the scheme. Gardner-Webb supplied offensive linemen familiar to Reisert. Ohio State is where Jacobs played as a long snapper and offensive lineman from 1997-2001. The guide also records Cory Smith from Penn State.
Toledo Rockets.portal_recruiting: The rebuilding mechanism, and the guide explains it rather than treating it as a surprise: Candle left as many of his players were running out of eligibility, and a head coach leaving opens the portal completely. 247Sports lists 37 transfers for Toledo, the third-best MAC class in its ranking.
Toledo Rockets.vsin_assessment: A strong claim made for a coach from an unusual route. The Coaching Carousel cites the 94-23 record, back-to-back FCS Playoff appearances, one of the nation's best defenses at Mercer in 2024 and nearly 500 yards per game on offense in 2025, then makes its case in market terms: given Candle's inability to do what needs to be done as a favorite, this could end up being quite the upgrade. The team pages call it something of a step up for the 47-year-old while making the same strong claim — he may well be an upgrade on Candle, which they note is hard to say about a coach who won 65% of his games overall and 68% in conference. They expect a slow start and warn the opener against Michigan State may not be pretty.
Toledo Rockets.strengths: A head coach at 94-23 with back-to-back FCS playoff appearances and a defense and offense that both ranked among the best at that level, a regionally coherent staff of northwest Ohio and Cleveland natives with Division II head-coaching experience, the third-best portal class in the MAC at 37 transfers, and a core of Mercer players who already know both schemes.
Toledo Rockets.concerns: A Stability Score of 0 with six returning starters and virtually no recognisable names — the top returning tackler at 35 tackles and the top returnee in yards of any kind at 194 receiving yards — a defense that allowed just 13.3 points and 96 rushing yards per game now rebuilt entirely, and a scheme the guide notes can be burned for explosive passes.
Toledo Rockets.betting: The Coaching Carousel frames the upgrade in market terms — Candle's inability to do what needs to be done as a favorite. The team pages conclude Jacobs seems like a good hire, with at least some familiarity thanks to transfers from a team that finished in the FCS Top 25 in each of the last two seasons, and project 8.04 wins.

Western Michigan Broncos.previous_hc_experience: Not addressed in guide. The guide records Lance Taylor's 10-15 start over his first two seasons in Kalamazoo before last year's breakthrough.
Western Michigan Broncos.dc: Greer Martini, 30, promoted from linebackers coach after Chris O'Leary returned to Jim Harbaugh's Chargers staff as defensive coordinator.
Western Michigan Broncos.oc_status: Returning — the Stability Score table (p. 44) awards 3 points for a returning offensive coordinator.
Western Michigan Broncos.dc_status: New — the guide records O'Leary's departure and Martini's promotion, and the Stability Score table (p. 44) awards 0 points for a returning defensive coordinator.
Western Michigan Broncos.play_caller: Not addressed in guide by name.
Western Michigan Broncos.offensive_scheme: Described distinctly. The guide calls it something of a throwback under coordinator Walt Bell, running double tight ends, and says it worked — Western Michigan played keep-away at 4.6 yards per carry.
Western Michigan Broncos.defensive_scheme: Not addressed as a named scheme. The guide quantifies what O'Leary built: tied for fourth nationally with 43 sacks, +21 in sack differential, 12th in third-down defense, and only 24 red-zone trips allowed across nine conference games.
Western Michigan Broncos.tempo: Deliberately slow — the guide describes the team playing keep-away and ranking 12th in average time of possession.
Western Michigan Broncos.run_pass: Heavily run-weighted, and the guide places it in national context: over 600 rushing attempts, seventh in total rush attempts nationally, behind only three service academies, Rice and Indiana. It explains the 109th ranking in yards per play as a function of that distribution.
Western Michigan Broncos.qb_development: Not addressed as a record. The guide records Broc Lowry returning as the conference's Offensive Player of the Year after 1,803 passing yards and 963 rushing with 23 total touchdowns, and identifies his running as the separator both for the offense and for him personally in taking the job full-time after an early-season timeshare.
Western Michigan Broncos.continuity: Head coach, offensive coordinator and quarterback return; the defensive coordinator changes but is promoted from within. The Stability Score table (p. 44) prints 4, 3, 0 and 4, plus 2 for 10 returning starters, totalling 13.
Western Michigan Broncos.staff_turnover: Confined to the defensive coordinator, and the guide treats the loss as significant: O'Leary left the Chargers for a year to call plays in Kalamazoo and has now returned to Jim Harbaugh's staff as defensive coordinator. It rates Martini's linebacker unit really good while noting the staff had to work the portal to replace departing players.
Western Michigan Broncos.prior_school: The Los Angeles Chargers, for both O'Leary's arrival and departure — and the guide notes Nadame Tucker's 14.5 sacks earned him an undrafted free agent deal from O'Leary and the Chargers.
Western Michigan Broncos.portal_recruiting: Asymmetric by design, and the guide names it directly: using the portal for depth rather than impact is a luxury, and that is the case on offense, but the defense is a major work in progress.
Western Michigan Broncos.vsin_assessment: A championship-caliber foundation with the credit for it assigned elsewhere. The guide builds its case on rarity — returning the conference's Offensive Player of the Year, at quarterback, plus a 1,000-yard back — and treats the Broncos as expected to make a strong run at repeating. Its honest accounting of how the wins came is that Western Michigan managed only 5.2 yards per play, helped by a +9 turnover margin, with a defense it calls spectacular. It credits the defensive improvement squarely to Chris O'Leary, who cut 1.4 yards per play off units that had allowed 6.4 and 6.1 in Taylor's first two seasons, and qualifies the offense with 12th in time of possession against a tie for 98th in plays of 10-plus yards and 110th in plays of 20-plus. Its conclusion is that there seem to be many reasons for scepticism given heavy personnel losses on defense and the loss of an NFL-calibre coordinator.
Western Michigan Broncos.strengths: The conference's returning Offensive Player of the Year at quarterback plus a 1,000-yard back, offensive-coordinator continuity in a distinctive and effective throwback scheme, a pretty experienced offensive line, portal depth used as a luxury on offense, and a promoted coordinator whose own linebacker unit the guide rates really good.
Western Michigan Broncos.concerns: The loss of an NFL-calibre defensive coordinator and of two pass rushers who combined for 21.5 sacks and 26 quarterback hits from a unit tied for fourth nationally, only 5.2 yards per play with few explosive plays, a +9 turnover margin unlikely to repeat, and a durability worry about a 6-foot-1 quarterback who carried 203 times with little depth behind him.
Western Michigan Broncos.betting: Not addressed in guide as an explicit market recommendation tied to coaching. Its coaching-linked conclusion is scepticism, given the defensive personnel losses and the coordinator's departure.
